newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria plods on one year after Ogoni hangings.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria plods on one year after Ogoni hangings.

text.p: Nigeria appears to have weathered the diplomatic storm that hit one year ago when it defied international opinion and hanged nine human rights activists.
The execution of Author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogoni minority rights activists for murder on November 10, 1995 instantly turned Africa's most populous nation into an international outcast.
It was suspended from the Commonwealth and a myriad of other sanctions followed in quick succession.
"The atmosphere now is certainly less tense than this time last year," commented an African diplomat who arrived in Nigeria at the time of the trial of the Ogoni nine.
It was as if international impatience with Nigeria, which had been building since 1993 when the army annulled a poll meant to restore democracy, suddenly snapped.

World leaders led by President Nelson Mandela of South Africa, who was emerging a moral force on the continent, castigated Nigeria's military rulers and promised to mobilise international pressure to force them to democratise and respect human rights.

But attempts to forge worldwide action on Nigeria fell apart when Western nations that buy Nigerian crude oil could not agree on an oil embargo, the only weapon many thought was capable of bringing the African nation to its knees.
"Oil is key to Nigeria's economic survival and without an oil embargo the rest of the sanctions are meaningless," said pro-democracy activist Lanre Shittu.
The Ogoni crisis itself was rooted in oil.

Saro-Wiwa led a pressure group that had long campaigned for self-determination for his 500,000-strong Ogoni tribe in the oil-producing southeastern Nigeria and which also demanded compensation from oil firms for environmental pollution.

The campaign, waged mainly from abroad, irritated Nigerian rulers and in 1994, Saro-Wiwa and many Ogoni activists were arrested when youths of his Movement for the Survival of Ogoni Peoples butchered four prominent Ogoni chiefs.
Nine were convicted by tribunal in a trial widely regarded as unfair and were swiftly hanged. Another 19 are still detained pending trial on the same murder charges.
Human rights groups say despite the international uproar over the hangings, the rights situation in multi-ethnic Nigeria has not improved.
Many people remain in detention, including Moshood Abiola, the wealthy businessman presumed to have won the 1993 poll who defied the military in 1994 and proclaimed himself president.
Opposition in the country has been significantly weakened by the fear of detention and many anti-government elements have chosen self-exile.

"As we remember the hanging of the Ogoni 9 today, the government must build bridges across ethnic groups and must assuage the feelings of minority groups," wrote the Sunday Concorde newspaper in an editorial.
But in the run-up to the anniversary of the hangings demonstrations were banned and opposition groups, fearing confrontation with security forces, opted for church services to remember Saro-Wiwa.
"Ogoni itself is calm," insists Fidelis Agbiki, the spokesman for the military administration in Rivers state that contains Ogoni.

"The press has not had the courage to tell the truth about Ogoni and that is why any time someone issues a statement saying so many Ogonis have been arrested, they just flash it without checking whether it is true," he told Reuters.
Nigerian rulers consider any foreign pressure as interference in the country's internal affairs and are plodding on with their own programme to hand over to an elected president in 1998.

Local newspapers are awash with reports that General Sani Abacha could contest the 1998 poll and succeed himself as an elected president, speculation that refuses to die despite his repeated pledge that the military will quit power.
Whether this will happen, as in other West African nations where military rulers became civilian leaders in what critics considered sham elections, may not be know until the last minute.
"We know in Nigeria you can expect anything," said one African ambassador.
